text:
Detroit outshot Seattle 40 to 24 and out-attempted them 82 to 53, and still lost 6-3. The Red Wings were the better team by the measures that travel well from game to game: 3.79 expected goals to 3.27, and a 58 percent share of simulated replays. Over the whole game that gap looks modest. The second period is where it fell apart, and it fell apart on the scoreboard far more than in the chances.

William Wallinder put Detroit up 2-1 at 4:00 of the second, on a 2 percent chance. Then Seattle scored four times in 9:05. Frederick Gaudreau tied it 39 seconds later, Mackie Samoskevich made it 3-2, Gaudreau scored again at 7:44, and Ben Meyers made it 5-2 at 14:05. Detroit generated 1.10 expected goals in that period to Seattle's 0.95, so the home side wasn't being overrun. John Gibson allowed five goals on 15 shots against 1.98 expected, about three goals worse than the chances warranted, and Daniil Tarasov replaced him.

At the other end, Philipp Grubauer faced 40 shots and stopped 37, a little better than the 3.79 expected goals he saw. Seattle also blocked 22 shots to Detroit's 12. Vince Dunn's power-play goal in the third made it 6-2, and Michael Brandsegg-Nygård's late goal, a 52 percent chance, only trimmed the margin. Seattle's even-strength expected goals were 2.3, yet they scored five times at even strength. Gaudreau (two goals) earned first star, with Meyers (a goal and two assists) and Berkly Catton (a goal and an assist) behind him.
